intro: Westerham is a small market town on the North Downs in west Kent, and just south of it, on a wooded hillside, lies Chartwell, Winston Churchill's family home from 1924 and now the National Trust's. In its grounds a reader photographed a giant sequoia rising straight above the broadleaves near the house and sent it to us. We do not yet know its age or size, and we would like to.

trees.story:
Chartwell, on the wooded hillside south of Westerham in Kent, was Winston Churchill's family home from 1924, and the National Trust opened its house and gardens to visitors after his death. A reader walking there in November sent us this giant sequoia, with a GPS fix taken a short way from the house.

The photograph looks up from a path deep in fallen leaves, through the branches of the trees in front, and the sequoia is the one that keeps going. Its trunk is red-brown and straight as a column, flaring at the foot where it meets the slope, and it climbs clear above the yellowing broadleaves around it before its dark, dense crown begins. In late autumn, when everything else in the picture has turned gold and copper, the sequoia stays green.

Giant sequoias reached Britain from the Sierra Nevada in 1853 and were planted on country estates all over Victorian England, where many now stand above every other tree around them. We do not know when this one was planted, or by whom, or how tall it has grown. If you know, or have measured its girth, tell us here and we will add your figures.

Stop on the path below it and follow the trunk up with your eyes until it clears the other trees.

faq.q: Can I visit The Chartwell Sequoia?

faq.q: Where at Chartwell is the sequoia?
faq.a: Near the house, beside a garden path on the slope, where its red-brown trunk rises above the broadleaves around it.
